analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from permanently replacing workers who strike or exercise union rights.
analysis.headline: The Senate majority fell short twice: cloture failed 55-41 and 57-42, short of the 60 votes needed, so the bill never got a final up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under long-standing labor law, an employer whose workers go on strike can hire permanent replacements and effectively take their jobs. This bill would make that an unfair labor practice under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act, and would bar employers from giving hiring preference to people who worked during a strike over workers who exercised their union rights and offered to return to work. The bill cleared the Senate Labor Committee but died on two failed votes to cut off debate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in unionized workplaces and railroad and airline employees. The bill would let them strike — or organize — without risking permanent loss of their jobs, restoring leverage that a 1938 Supreme Court decision (NLRB v. Mackay Radio) gave employers when it allowed hiring permanent replacements for economic strikers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unionized workers and railroad and airline employees

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to offer or grant permanent-replacement status to anyone performing bargaining-unit work during a labor dispute.
Bars employers from giving any employment preference to someone who worked, or offered to work, during a dispute over an employee who exercised union rights and has offered to return to work.
Applies the same ban to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act, prohibiting carriers from discriminating against employees who engaged in the dispute.

The committee-reported version covered employees in bargaining units where a union was the certified representative or was seeking certification on the basis of signed authorizations from a majority of unit employees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces, and rail and air carriers. They would lose the ability to keep operating indefinitely by permanently replacing strikers, and would face unfair-labor-practice liability if they did. Some employers argue this shifts bargaining power sharply toward unions and raises the risk of prolonged strikes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unionized employers and rail and air carriers

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose a long-standing lawful means of keeping operations running during a strike; opponents argue this hands unions greater leverage to sustain strikes and could prolong disputes that consumers and other workers depend on.
The Executive Branch objected: the Departments of Labor, Commerce, and Transportation submitted unfavorable comments to the committee.

The committee-reported substitute narrowed the bill from the original, limiting it to workers in unionized units or units where a union was seeking certification — so many nonunion workers would get no new protection.
A minority of committee members filed minority views against the bill when it was reported.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers it covers, the bill addressed a real imbalance: today an employee who lawfully strikes can be permanently replaced, which makes the right to strike largely symbolic. The cost falls on employers, who lose a tool for operating through disputes, and critics fairly warn that could invite more and longer strikes. The committee version also narrowed the protection, leaving most nonunion workers with nothing. On balance it would have materially strengthened ordinary workers' bargaining power at a genuine cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee but, when the Senate took it up in June 1992, it failed two cloture votes — 55-41 and 57-42, both short of the 60 needed to cut off debate — so it never received a final vote and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Metzenbaum on January 14, 1991, with 36 cosponsors (34 Democrats, 2 Republicans), and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The Labor Subcommittee held hearings in March 1991.
The committee received unfavorable executive comments from the Departments of Labor, Commerce, and Transportation.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was reported on July 18, 1991 with minority views filed, then placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate took up the measure in June 1992; the first cloture vote on the committee substitute failed 55-41, with 50 of 57 Democrats voting yes and only 5 of 43 Republicans.
After the substitute was modified, a second cloture vote failed 57-42, again falling short of the 60 votes needed to end debate and reach final passage.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 without the bill receiving a final vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with unionized workforces and the rail and air carriers came out ahead: they retain the ability to permanently replace striking workers and face no new liability. The 38 senators who voted against ending debate both times preserved that ability.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unionized employers and rail and air carriers

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Labor Committee.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA), chair of the Labor and Human Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with a substitute amendment and managed it on the floor.

for.name: 50 of 57 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate Democratic caucus members voting on cloture
for.what_they_did: Voted to end debate and bring the bill to a final vote, both times.

for.name: 36 cosponsors including Sen. Mark Hatfield
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including two Republicans.

against.what_they_did: Voted against ending debate on both cloture votes, keeping the bill from a final vote.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush

against.what_they_did: Submitted unfavorable executive comments on the bill to the Labor Committee.

sides.party_line_note: On the first cloture vote, 50 of 57 Democrats voted yes while only 5 of 43 Republicans did; the second vote was nearly identical at 52-5 among Democrats and 5-37 among Republicans, with a small Democratic minority of 5 joining the opposition each time.

industries.industry: Unionized employers (private-sector businesses with union contracts)
industries.note: Because the bill died, they keep the right under NLRB v. Mackay Radio to permanently replace economic strikers, which weakens workers' leverage in negotiations. Their interest ran against the workers' interest in job security during a lawful strike.

industries.industry: Railroads and airlines (carriers under the Railway Labor Act)
industries.note: The bill would have barred carriers from replacing or discriminating against employees who engage in transport labor disputes; its failure preserves their ability to hire replacements.
Unions pushed for the bill because permanent replacement of strikers undermines the strike as a bargaining tool. Its failure leaves that leverage gap in place.
